title: Clerical life: Call me by my name
gist: An Anglican priest describes deliberately dropping honorific titles for clergy over the last 15 years and argues the Church of England's 'Title + First Name' convention (e.g. 'Bishop Hugh') has crept downward into a rigid, uncodified hierarchy that she connects to institutional insecurity following clerical abuse scandals.

insights.claim: The author observes that institutions invoke 'the dignity of the office' to justify formal titles specifically when that dignity has already been comprehensively undermined—in the Church of England's case, by clerical abuse scandals and treatment of LGBTQ people.
insights.speaker: Alice Goodman
insights.so_what: A transferable organizational-behaviour insight: escalating formal status rituals within an institution can be a leading indicator of underlying reputational or legitimacy crisis, applicable well beyond the Church.
insights.locator: The first is that you only do things for “the dignity of the office”

insights.claim: Over roughly the last 15 years, the Church of England has adopted a 'Title plus First Name' address convention (e.g. 'Bishop Hugh', 'Archdeacon Richard') that has spread downward through the clerical hierarchy from bishops to deans, archdeacons and rectors, replacing older bare-title forms of address.
insights.speaker: Alice Goodman
insights.so_what: Documents a specific, dateable shift in institutional norms within the Church of England, useful context for anyone tracking internal culture/status dynamics in the institution.
insights.locator: The second quibble is the way that the “Title + First Name” pattern

insights.claim: The author argues the modern clerical title convention creates an asymmetric hierarchy dressed as informal friendliness: senior clergy address juniors by first name only, while juniors are expected to use the senior's title plus first name, with honour flowing consistently upward despite the appearance of camaraderie.
insights.speaker: Alice Goodman
insights.so_what: A useful framework for spotting disguised hierarchy in any organization that presents itself as flat or informal while maintaining strict rank-based deference norms underneath.
insights.quote: Honour is sucked upwards in this world, in the draft of “the dignity of the office.”
insights.locator: When you’re addressed by a senior colleague

insights.claim: This hierarchical title expectation is entirely uncodified within the Church of England—not found in Crockford's Clerical Directory's official guidance on addressing the clergy—yet has been consistently observed by everyone for around 15 years, akin to an unwritten convention like the British constitution.
insights.speaker: Alice Goodman
insights.so_what: Illustrates how informal, unwritten norms can become as binding as formal rules within an institution—relevant to understanding culture change and status enforcement in hierarchical organizations generally.
insights.quote: This expectation, like the British constitution, remains uncodified.
insights.locator: It’s not in the front section of Crockford’s

insights.claim: The author personally decided to stop addressing any Church of England clergy—bishops, archdeacons, deans, canons—by anything beyond their Christian name, while still using formal titles for leaders of other churches (e.g. the Pope, the Ecumenical Patriarch) as a sign of ecumenical respect.
insights.speaker: Alice Goodman
insights.so_what: A small but pointed example of individual, low-cost resistance to perceived institutional status inflation—illustrative of how individuals within hierarchies can signal dissent without open confrontation.
insights.quote: One morning recently I woke up and knew that never again would I call a bishop of the Church of England... by anything beyond their Christian name.
insights.locator: Call me Ishmael. I mean, call me Alice
